elements.quote: Methods A systematic review of the literature was conducted by searching PubMed, the Excerpta Medica Database (Embase, via OvidSP), Scopus and Web of Science, covering publications from inception to April 2024.
elements.reason: The abstract explicitly states that a systematic review of the literature was conducted.

elements.quote: This meta-­ analysis aimed to evaluate the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome among children and adolescents.
elements.reason: The abstract clearly states the main objective/review question.

elements.quote: Studies were included if they evaluated the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome among children and adolescents.
elements.reason: The abstract states the main inclusion criterion but does not report any exclusion criteria in the abstract.

elements.quote: Methods A systematic review of the literature was conducted by searching PubMed, the Excerpta Medica Database (Embase, via OvidSP), Scopus and Web of Science, covering publications from inception to April 2024.
elements.reason: The abstract lists the information sources searched and states the date range/last search (to April 2024).
The abstract does not report any methods used to assess risk of bias in included studies.

elements.quote: A random-­ effects model was used to estimate the summary effect size.
elements.reason: The abstract specifies the synthesis method (random-effects model) used to present and combine results.

elements.quote: A total of eight studies involving children and adolescents aged 6 to 19 years were included in the meta-­ analysis (n=6562, 50% girls).
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies and participants and gives a brief participant characteristic (age range, percent girls).

elements.quote: Low adherence to the Mediterranean diet was associated with greater odds of metabolic syndrome than was medium/high adherence (odds ratio [OR] = 2.18, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.45 to 3.28; p < 0.001; inconsistency index [ I 2 ] = 64.15%).
elements.reason: The abstract presents the main outcome result including effect estimate, CI, p-value and heterogeneity statistic.

elements.quote: Low adherence to the Mediterranean diet was associated with greater odds of metabolic syndrome than was medium/high adherence (odds ratio [OR] = 2.18, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.45 to 3.28; p < 0.001; inconsistency index [ I 2 ] = 64.15%).
elements.reason: A summary estimate from the meta-analysis (OR) with its 95% confidence interval is reported in the abstract.

elements.quote: Low adherence to the Mediterranean diet was associated with greater odds of metabolic syndrome than was medium/high adherence
elements.reason: The abstract indicates the direction of effect (low adherence associated with greater odds) and which group is favoured (medium/high adherence is associated with lower odds).
The abstract does not briefly summarize limitations of the included evidence (risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision) within the abstract text.

elements.quote: Conclusion This meta-­ analysis suggested that increased adherence to a Mediterranean diet is associated with lower probabilities of having cardiometabolic risk among children and adolescents. Thus, our findings suggest that public health strategies are needed to implement and promote effective actions toward healthy eating habits in children and adolescents.
elements.reason: The abstract provides a general interpretation of the results and notes implications for public health.
The abstract does not specify the primary source of funding for the review.
The abstract does not provide the register name or registration number; registration is reported elsewhere in the manuscript but not in the abstract.

elements.quote: Background The Mediterranean diet has been associated with improved metabolic health among adults. This meta-­ analysis aimed to evaluate the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome among children and adolescents.
elements.reason: The abstract states the existing knowledge (association in adults) and frames the review aim to evaluate this association in children/adolescents, indicating the current state of knowledge and the uncertainty in younger populations.

elements.quote: This meta-­ analysis aimed to evaluate the association between adherence to a Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome among children and adolescents.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly explains the purpose/need for the review by stating it aims to evaluate the association in children and adolescents, implying the importance of addressing this question in that population.
No text in the provided evidence discusses existing systematic reviews, the need for the current review relative to prior reviews, or cites previous reviews.
This review assesses associations between diet adherence and metabolic syndrome (observational), not effects of an intervention; the requirement to describe an intervention mechanism does not apply.
The review does not evaluate a complex intervention or delivery context, so a logic model is not applicable.

No explicit statement of the review objectives or research question is present in the retrieved evidence. The provided chunks describe methods, eligibility criteria, and findings but do not include an explicit objectives or question statement.

elements.quote: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had an adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross-­ sectional study design.
elements.reason: This review examines associations in observational (cross-sectional and longitudinal) studies of adherence to the Mediterranean diet and metabolic syndrome rather than effects of interventions; therefore PICO-style planned comparisons for intervention effects are not applicable.

elements.quote: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had a adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross-­ sectional study design.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies key study characteristics used to determine eligibility (age range, population scope, outcome of interest, requirement for validated MedDiet assessment, and eligible study designs).

elements.quote: A search strategy was used to identify all eligible studies published before 22 April 2024.
elements.reason: The report specifies a search cut-off date (dissemination timing). Language restriction is reported elsewhere ('we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English'), but publication/report status (eg, unpublished data, grey literature) is not described, so the reporting of report characteristics is incomplete.
No evidence was provided that the review distinguished excluding studies because outcomes were not measured from excluding studies because outcome results were not reported.

elements.quote: Children and adolescents with low adherence to the MedDiet had greater odds of developing MetS compared to those with medium to high adherence.
elements.reason: The syntheses are defined by comparison groups (low adherence vs medium-to-high adherence) linked to the review objective of association between MedDiet adherence and MetS.

elements.quote: However, to narrow the scope of the meta-­ analysis, only studies that associated the MedDiet with the outcome of MetS were included.
elements.reason: A rationale for a notable restriction (limiting the meta-analysis to studies that directly associated MedDiet with MetS) is explicitly provided.

elements.quote: The searches included studies published from database inception to 22 April 2024.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the date to which the searches were conducted ('...to 22 April 2024'), indicating when the information sources were last searched.

elements.quote: Two authors independently conducted systematic searches in the following databases: Excerpta Medica Database (Embase, via OvidSP), Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed. The searches included studies published from database inception to 22 April 2024.
elements.reason: The names of the bibliographic databases are listed, the platform/interface is specified for Embase ('via OvidSP'), and coverage dates are given as 'from database inception to 22 April 2024.'
No study registers, regulatory databases, or online repositories are reported as being searched in the evidence, so this item does not apply.
No websites, search engines, or other online sources (with names or URLs) are reported as searched in the provided evidence.

The report does not name any organisations or manufacturers that were contacted to identify studies; only that a professional librarian was consulted and authors of included studies were contacted for missing information.

elements.quote: In cases where missing information was identified in the published paper, the relevant authors of those studies were contacted directly to request the missing information.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies the type of individuals contacted ('relevant authors of those studies') to obtain missing information.

elements.quote: The reference lists of eligible studies were manually examined to find further relevant papers and included if suitable.
elements.reason: The types of reference lists examined are specified as the reference lists of eligible studies, and that these were manually examined.
Although reference lists were manually examined, no details are provided about backward/forward citation searching (seed reports, citation index/platform, or search date).
No journals or conference proceedings consulted (with source names, dates covered, or search methods) are reported in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: The complete search strategies used for all the databases are presented in online supplemental file 2.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that the complete search strategies for all databases are provided in an online supplemental file.

elements.quote: The searches included studies published from database inception to 22 April 2024. The search was limited to peer-­ reviewed studies published in English.
elements.reason: Search limits (date range and language/peer-reviewed restriction) are described, but no justification is provided linking these limits to the eligibility criteria.
No citation of published search approaches or filters nor description of any adaptations is provided in the available evidence.
The evidence contains no mention of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools used to identify or refine search terms.
No tools used to translate search strings between sources are specified in the provided text.
There is no description of any validation of the search strategy, validation processes, or validation studies in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: A professional librarian was consulted to ensure the quality of the search strategy.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports consultation with a professional librarian (a form of peer input), but does not describe the peer-review process or specify a tool (e.g., PRESS).

elements.quote: The search strategy included controlled vocabulary terms specific to each database along with keywords derived from scoping index articles relevant to this meta-­ analysis. The following terms related to the MedDiet were used: MEDdiet, Mediterranean Diet Quality Index for Children and Adolescents (KIDMED) score, MedDiet score, MedDiet and hypertension, MedDiet and diabetes, KIDMED and MedDiet score. The following outcome terms related to MetS were included: MetS or components (hyperlipidaemia, hypertriglyceridaemia, insulin resistance, hyperglycaemia, hypertension) combined with health.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the conceptual structure and the terms/approach used to develop the search (controlled vocabulary, keywords, and specific search terms).

elements.quote: Two authors (VPD and AG-­ H) thoroughly examined the entire texts of identified publications for eligibility after removing duplicates and systematically reviewed the titles and abstracts of eligible manuscripts.
elements.reason: The manuscript states that two authors performed the examination of full texts and titles/abstracts, reporting the number of reviewers involved in screening stages.

elements.quote: Two authors independently conducted systematic searches in the following databases: Excerpta Medica Database (Embase, via OvidSP), Scopus, Web of Science and PubMed.
elements.reason: The paper explicitly reports that two authors worked independently for the search process, but it does not explicitly state that screening of records and full reports was carried out independently at each screening stage (screening language for independence of title/abstract and full-text screening is not explicit).

elements.quote: In case of discrepancies or uncertainty regarding eligibility, a third reviewer (CA-­ S) was consulted to reach consensus.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes how disagreements about eligibility were resolved by consulting a third reviewer to reach consensus.

elements.quote: In cases where missing information was identified in the published paper, the relevant authors of those studies were contacted directly to request the missing information.
elements.reason: The authors report contacting study authors to obtain missing information, describing processes used to obtain or confirm study information from investigators.
No information was provided about methods used to translate abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment.

elements.quote: A total of 1456 studies were excluded because of duplication, while 1565 were classified as ineligible by automation tools.
elements.reason: The manuscript mentions that automation tools classified a number of records as ineligible but does not describe how automation tools were integrated into the selection process or provide details of their use.

Although automation tools are mentioned, no details identify externally derived classifiers by version or reference, nor is there reporting of records removed before screening attributable to such classifiers.
There is no information describing any internally derived classifiers, their training, validation, or use in selection.
No mention is made of machine-learning prioritisation tools or any screening stopping/prioritisation rules.
The manuscript provides no information on use of crowdsourcing platforms in study selection.
There is no report of previously screened datasets used to eliminate records or description of how such datasets were derived.

elements.quote: Similarly, outcome measures varied, with most studies using International Diabetes Federation (IDF) criteria for defining MetS, while some also included definitions based on homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) or other phenotype-based approaches (eg, metabolically unhealthy obesity [MUO]).
elements.reason: The manuscript lists and describes the outcome domains (MetS and its components) and the definitions/approaches used across studies (IDF, HOMA-IR, MUO).
No evidence specifies the time frame of measurement for each outcome domain (no time points or measurement windows for MetS or components are reported in the provided text).

elements.quote: All results from each study that were compatible with each outcome domain were included.
elements.reason: The Methods explicitly state that all compatible results from each study were sought and included.
Not applicable because the authors report they included all compatible results (so no selection process for subsets of results was needed).
No information is provided about any changes to outcome-domain inclusion, definitions, or their importance, nor any rationales for such changes.
No information is provided about changes to processes for selecting results within eligible outcome domains or rationales for such changes.
The manuscript does not report which outcomes were considered most important for interpreting conclusions nor provide a rationale for any prioritisation.

elements.quote: The following information was extracted from the included studies: (a) reference (year); (b) country; (c) characteristics of the subjects, including total sample size, sex ratio, age range and mean age; (d) type of questionnaire used; and (e) outcome information, including information on MetS and adherence to the MedDiet.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly lists the additional variables extracted (reference, country, participant characteristics including sample size, sex ratio, age range and mean age, questionnaire type, and outcome information on MetS and MedDiet adherence).

elements.quote: In cases where missing information was identified in the published paper, the relevant authors of those studies were contacted directly to request the missing information.
elements.reason: The authors describe how they sought to obtain missing information (contacting study authors) but do not describe any assumptions made about missing or unclear information (for example, how unresolved missing data were handled or any imputation/assumptions applied).

elements.quote: The extracted data were systematised via a specially constructed standardised data extraction form (see study protocol), and the extracted data were then reviewed for consistency by the reviewers.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports using a specially constructed standardised data extraction form (and refers to the study protocol), indicating a tool was used to determine/collect data items.

elements.quote: Each included study was independently reviewed for critical appraisal and bias reduction, and a modified version of the Newcastle Ottawa cohort scale was used for cross-­ sectional research (online supplemental file 1).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly names the risk-of-bias tool used (a modified Newcastle Ottawa cohort scale) in text_11.

elements.quote: Representativeness of the sample | Sample size | Non-­ respondents | Ascertainment of exposure | Based on design and analysis | Assessment of outcome | test
elements.reason: The table (table_0) lists specific domains/items (representativeness, sample size, non-respondents, ascertainment of exposure, comparability, assessment of outcome, statistical test) assessed by the tool.
No statement was found describing whether an overall risk-of-bias judgement was made nor the rules used to derive any overall judgement.

elements.quote: a modified version of the Newcastle Ottawa cohort scale was used for cross-­ sectional research (online supplemental file 1).
elements.reason: The manuscript indicates the tool was modified but does not describe what adaptations were made to the Newcastle-Ottawa scale.
No newly developed risk-of-bias tool is reported; the study used a (modified) existing Newcastle-Ottawa tool.

elements.quote: Each included study was independently reviewed for critical appraisal and bias reduction... Consensus was used to settle disagreements;
elements.reason: The manuscript states studies were independently reviewed and that consensus was used to resolve disagreements, but it does not specify the number of reviewers performing the risk-of-bias assessments.

elements.quote: In cases where missing information was identified in the published paper, the relevant authors of those studies were contacted directly to request the missing information.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes contacting study authors to obtain missing information, which addresses processes used to obtain/confirm information from investigators.
No information is provided about use, training, performance, validation, or any use of automation tools specifically for risk-of-bias assessment.

elements.quote: The effect size of each study was evaluated using the odds ratio (OR) and its 95% confidence interval (CI).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the effect measure used (odds ratio with 95% CI) for the association between MedDiet adherence and MetS.

No thresholds or ranges for interpreting effect size (e.g., what constitutes small/medium/large OR) or rationale for such thresholds are reported in the provided evidence. The only thresholds reported relate to I2 heterogeneity, not effect size interpretation.
There is no description in the provided evidence of methods to re-express synthesized results using another effect measure.
The provided evidence specifies the effect measure used but does not provide any justification for choosing odds ratios over other effect measures.

elements.quote: To be eligible for inclusion in the present review, studies needed to meet the following criteria: (i) were children or adolescents aged 5-19 years, all countries and ethnic backgrounds; (ii) had a MetS outcome; (iii) had an adherence to the MedDiet assessed by a validated questionnaire; and (iv) had a longitudinal and cross-­ sectional study design. However, to narrow the scope of the meta-­ analysis, only studies that associated the MedDiet with the outcome of MetS were included. In contrast, the exclusion criteria included adults and adolescents/children with evidence of metabolic or autoimmune liver disease, diabetes or the presence of known systemic disease. Studies were also excluded if they presented duplicate data from the same source and year. When two studies used duplicate data from the same source and year, the study with the larger sample size was selected.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies inclusion and exclusion criteria and explicitly states that the meta-analysis was limited to studies associating MedDiet with MetS, describing how studies were selected for the synthesis.

elements.quote: A meta-­ analysis was also conducted to investigate the associations between MetS and MedDiet adherence. To determine the overall estimated OR and its related 95% CIs, the random-­ effects inverse variance model with the traditional DerSimonian and Laird method was used. To measure the percentage of disparities across studies, we used the inconsistency index ( I 2 ), which was calculated with the Cochran Q statistic. I 2 values of 0%-40%, 30%-60%, 50%-90% and 75%--100% were considered cut-­ off values for non-­ important, moderate, substantial and considerable degrees of inconsistency, respectively.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the statistical synthesis approach (random-effects inverse variance model, DerSimonian and Laird method, and I2/Cochran Q for heterogeneity), which addresses preparation for meta-analysis. However, it provides limited information on specific data-preparation steps (e.g., explicit data conversions or formulas used, handling of missing summary statistics). Although the authors note that they contacted study authors for missing information (text_10) and mention that data conversion was required as a limitation (text_20), no detailed methods for conversions or handling missing summary statistics are reported, so the requirement is only partially met.

No methods text describes the tabular structures used to display results or the data included in them; only tables themselves are presented without a methodological description of their structure in the Methods or Synthesis sections.

elements.quote: Publication bias was assessed via a funnel plot, and Egger's test was used for the assessment of bias.
elements.reason: The Methods explicitly state a graphical method (funnel plot) was used to display/assess publication bias.
There is no statement describing the basis for ordering or grouping studies within tables or graphs (e.g., by year, sample size, effect size, or study design).

elements.quote: Figure 2 Results of the individual studies. τ ², heteogeneity; I ², inconsistency index.
elements.reason: Only standard graphs are reported (e.g., a forest-plot-style presentation in Figure 2 and funnel plot for publication bias); no non-standard graphs are used and no rationale for non-standard graphs is needed.

elements.quote: All analyses were conducted using Stata version 17.0 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA).
elements.reason: The software and version used for statistical synthesis is explicitly reported (Stata v17.0).
A meta-analysis was performed (reported throughout), so description of alternative synthesis methods when meta-analysis was not possible does not apply.

elements.quote: To determine the overall estimated OR and its related 95% CIs, the random-­ effects inverse variance model with the traditional DerSimonian and Laird method was used.
elements.reason: The meta-analysis model is reported (random-effects inverse-variance, DerSimonian–Laird). However, an explicit rationale for choosing this model is not provided.

elements.quote: To determine the overall estimated OR and its related 95% CIs, the random-­ effects inverse variance model with the traditional DerSimonian and Laird method was used.
elements.reason: The statistical method used for meta-analysis is explicitly described (random-effects inverse-variance, DerSimonian–Laird).

elements.quote: To measure the percentage of disparities across studies, we used the inconsistency index ( I 2 ), which was calculated with the Cochran Q statistic. I 2 values of 0%-40%, 30%-60%, 50%-90% and 75%--100% were considered cut-­ off values for non-­ important, moderate, substantial and considerable degrees of inconsistency, respectively.
elements.reason: Methods to identify and quantify heterogeneity are reported: I² calculated from Cochran's Q with specified interpretive cutoffs.

elements.quote: the random-­ effects inverse variance model with the traditional DerSimonian and Laird method was used.
elements.reason: For the random-effects meta-analysis, the between-study variance estimator (DerSimonian–Laird) is specified.
No specific method for calculating confidence intervals for the summary effect (e.g., exact/normal approximation, Hartung-Knapp, etc.) is described; only 95% CIs are reported without method.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity: τ² = 0.21, /² = 64.15% | | | | Random-effects (DerSimonian-Laird model)
elements.reason: Some additional random-effects details are reported (numeric τ² and I² value shown in results and model named), but other implementation details (e.g., weighting scheme beyond inverse-variance, convergence criteria) are not described.
No Bayesian meta-analysis was conducted or reported, so priors are not applicable.
No methods are described for accounting for statistical dependency among multiple estimates from the same study (no evidence of multilevel/meta-regression or dependency adjustments).
The manuscript does not identify any planned syntheses that were judged impossible or inappropriate nor provide reasons; no evidence of reporting this is present.

elements.quote: A sensitivity analysis was conducted by sequentially omitting one study at a time to assess the robustness of the overall effect estimate.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes a sensitivity (leave-one-out) analysis to explore robustness and reports heterogeneity statistics in the meta-analysis, indicating methods to explore heterogeneity were used.
No subgroup analyses or meta-regression are described; no factors, factor levels, or expected directions of effect modification are reported in the supplied evidence.
The manuscript does not report whether analyses used study-level variables, within-study contrasts, or both; no text specifies the level of variables used for heterogeneity analyses.

elements.quote: A sensitivity analysis was conducted by sequentially omitting one study at a time to assess the robustness of the overall effect estimate.
elements.reason: No subgroup analyses were reported in the manuscript, so methods to compare subgroup effects do not apply.

elements.quote: To measure the percentage of disparities across studies, we used the inconsistency index ( I 2 ), which was calculated with the Cochran Q statistic.
elements.reason: A quantitative meta-analysis was performed (with I2 reported); the manuscript does not state that meta-analysis was unsuitable or that informal methods were used instead, so this conditional item does not apply.
The manuscript does not identify whether any heterogeneity analyses were post-hoc or not pre-specified; no statement distinguishing pre-specified vs exploratory analyses is provided in the evidence.

elements.quote: A sensitivity analysis was conducted by sequentially omitting one study at a time to assess the robustness of the overall effect estimate. The pooled ORs remained stable across all iterations, ranging from 1.91 to 2.43, and all remained statistically significant (p ≤ 0.001).
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the sensitivity analysis method (leave-one-out), reports the range of pooled ORs and significance, and table_3 lists the results for each omitted study, meeting the requirement to report details of the sensitivity analyses performed.
No evidence in the provided text indicates whether any sensitivity analyses were not pre-specified or identifies post-hoc analyses as such; pre-specification status is not reported.

elements.quote: Publication bias was assessed via a funnel plot, and Egger's test was used for the assessment of bias.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states the methods used to assess risk of bias due to missing results (funnel plot and Egger's test).
No information is provided about an existing assessment tool's specific domains or items or how an overall judgement was derived for reporting-bias assessment.
No descriptions of adaptations to any existing reporting-bias tool are reported in the provided evidence.
No newly developed reporting-bias tool is described or referenced in the manuscript; the authors report using standard methods (funnel plot, Egger's test).

elements.quote: Each included study was independently reviewed for critical appraisal and bias reduction, and a modified version of the Newcastle Ottawa cohort scale was used for cross-­ sectional research (online supplemental file 1). 29 Consensus was used to settle disagreements; the results are shown in table 1.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports independent review and that consensus was used to resolve disagreements, but does not report the number of reviewers involved for the reporting-bias assessment.

elements.quote: In cases where missing information was identified in the published paper, the relevant authors of those studies were contacted directly to request the missing information.
elements.reason: The authors describe contacting study authors to obtain missing information, which is a process to obtain or confirm relevant information from investigators.
No information is provided about use, training, performance, or validation of automation tools specifically for reporting-bias assessment.

elements.quote: A total of eight cross-­ sectional studies were included in the meta-­ analysis. elements.quote: These findings are consistent with previous research in adults, suggesting that adherence to the MedDiet may have favourable effects on MetS outcomes. 17 However, unlike the study performed by Bakaloudi et al , 17 our study focused only on children and adolescents, presenting a well-­ designed systematic review and meta-­ analysis of paediatric populations.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly situates the study's results relative to prior research (noting consistency with adult studies and contrasting with Bakaloudi et al), and further explains potential mechanisms and public-health implications, thereby interpreting the results in the context of other evidence.

elements.quote: Limitations of the present systematic review include the fact that the degree of adherence to the MedDiet could be subject to regional variations, potentially introducing further biases. For example, individuals with high adherence to the MedDiet living in Mediterranean areas may consume certain foods more frequently than may those residing in non-­ Mediterranean regions. Furthermore, the need to convert data for the purpose of quantitative analysis presents an additional limitation to our study; additionally, we restricted our inclusion criteria to studies published in English. In addition, most of the included studies were cross-­ sectional, which limits the ability to establish causality or determine the temporal relationship between adherence to the MedDiet and MetS outcomes. However, further well-­ designed prospective cohort studies and randomised controlled trials are needed to confirm the findings of our meta-­ analysis and elucidate the underlying mechanisms involved. All the studies used a cross-­ sectional design, so the observed results should be interpreted with caution. Another significant limitation is that studies use different questionnaires to determine adherence to the MedDiet, as well as different points for comparisons between categories. Additionally, there is no single criterion for defining MetS in the paediatric population, so the observed inconsistency could be due to these limitations. Finally, a formal assessment of the certainty of evidence (eg, using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation approach) was not performed, as this was beyond the scope of the present review.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly lists multiple limitations of the included evidence: regional variation in adherence measurement, data conversion, English-only inclusion, predominance of cross-sectional designs limiting causality, heterogeneous questionnaires and MetS definitions, and absence of a formal certainty assessment.
